extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate pre-service middle-grades mathematics teachers and instructors
extracted.subtask_description: Designing/participating in an undergraduate course for pre-service middle-grades teachers that emphasizes problem-solving, visualization, use of dynamic software (GSP), investigation, and open-ended assessment. The rubric covers learner expectations, classroom practices, content units, tools, and assessment philosophy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use dynamic software to aid in problem solving
rubrics_metrics.description: Students are expected to use dynamic software (e.g., Geometer's Sketchpad) to aid in problem solving.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: GSP is used to construct figures, take measurements (Measurement tool), drag vertices to test conjectures, and help students be more confident in conjectures; short lessons on using GSP are provided; many assignments and investigations require its use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use mathematical modeling to solve geometric problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Students should use mathematical modeling to solve geometric problems. The term “mathematical modeling” refers to the use of mathematics to aid in the solving of real-world problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modeling is an explicit expectation of the course and is embedded in problem-based activities and projects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make conjectures based on observations
rubrics_metrics.description: Students should make conjectures based on their observations of geometric phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conjectures arise from exploration (e.g., midpoint quadrilateral conjecture). Students are expected to test conjectures using tools like GSP and to consider what is needed to justify them; proofs are discussed but not the main focus—justification often emerges via instructor-led discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present clear and concise explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: Students should be able to present clear and concise explanations of their work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Class meetings include small-group work followed by group presentations to the class; groups are expected to answer questions from classmates; presentation and communication of strategies are integral to the course and motivate effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reason mathematically (investigate, communicate, generalize)
rubrics_metrics.description: Students should be able to reason mathematically: investigate, communicate, and generalize patterns and relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many tasks require collecting data, examining patterns (e.g., diagonals of prisms), and forming generalizations. Instructors assess the extent to which students justify their conjectures with mathematical evidence based on exploration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Active participation and collaborative problem solving
rubrics_metrics.description: Without the students’ active participation in solving and presenting problems, the class would not be what it is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical class meetings reserve most time for students working in small groups on activities; groups present solutions and engage in class discussion; collaborative tasks and peer verification are emphasized (e.g., exchanging polycube drawings to verify congruence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Bring and use course notes each meeting
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no required textbook; the course notes, including exercises, are made available and students are required to print and bring them to each class meeting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Course notes were adapted from Collier; printed notes are expected as part of class preparation and participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop visualization and multiple-representation skills
rubrics_metrics.description: A goal of the course is to improve students’ visualization skills and their ability to represent figures in multiple ways (nets, stack maps, isometric drawings, virtual manipulatives).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tools and activities include the National Library of Virtual Manipulatives applets, isometric dot paper, stack maps, nets, polyomino/polycube physical models (multilink cubes), and use of online applets to generate isometric views; instructors note common student difficulties and recommend resources or manipulatives to support learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand and use precise definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Students must understand precise definitions (e.g., polyomino, n-omino, building number, congruence correspondences) because definitions affect reasoning and outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discussions show how definitions impact problems (e.g., whether reflections are considered in congruence affects building numbers of polycubes); instructors prompt students to appreciate the role of definitions in counting and classification tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Express transformations functionally and determine transformation parameters
rubrics_metrics.description: Students should write isometries as functions (e.g., M_AB(P), R_Q;ABC(P), T_AB(P)) and be able to determine parameters (center and angle of rotation, line of reflection, translation vector).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises require writing correct functional expressions for reflections, rotations, and translations on geoboards; common student difficulty is understanding the functional notation and choosing appropriate preimage points when images don't fall on geoboard points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify types of congruence and compose transformations
rubrics_metrics.description: Students should determine whether congruent figures are related by reflection, rotation, translation, or compositions (e.g., glide reflections), and find the parameters for such correspondences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problems ask for all congruence correspondences and classification of congruence types, and for finding parameters for glide reflections or single transformations equivalent to compositions; students must reason about order and relative positions of components.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collect data, seek patterns, and generalize rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment items expect students to collect data, examine it for patterns, and generalize (e.g., determine a formula for number of diagonals of prisms/pyramids).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instructors design problems that do not tell students how to proceed; students are expected to recognize that collecting examples and generalizing is the method to solve such problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment philosophy: non-routine, minimal prompting, evidence-based justification
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment typically consists of assignments, projects, quizzes, and exams that pose non-routine problems; instructors try to provide as little information as possible so students must determine what to do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students are assessed on problem-solving, reasoning, extent and quality of justification for conjectures (often based on exploration with GSP), and ability to generalize; example exam items require explicit parameter specification and justification rather than procedural steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design and complete exploratory and long-term projects with classroom connection
rubrics_metrics.description: Assignments and long-term projects require exploration of mathematical topics (e.g., Pythagorean theorem investigations, transformation composition, fractals) and, for project work, reflection on use in middle-grades classrooms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Projects are open-ended (can cause anxiety); students should use GSP or manipulatives, make and justify conjectures, and for pedagogy projects, discuss potential classroom adaptations and applicability to middle school students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use physical manipulatives and varied tools appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of physical manipulatives (miras, tracing paper, geoboards, multilink cubes), virtual manipulatives, and apps is expected to support learning and visualization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instructors recommend manipulatives when drawing or visualizing is difficult; physical models help students gain experience determining congruence and visualizing reflections/rotations in space.
